references.text: The immediate context in John 1:37–38 shows that the two disciples followed Jesus after the Baptist's testimony, and Jesus asked them what they were seeking. Verse 39 is the answer to this: an invitation to personal experience and fellowship.
Philip says to Nathanael, 'Come and see' (John 1:46) — the same pattern as in verse 39, where the invitation to come and personally experience who Jesus is, is repeated.
The Samaritan woman uses similar wording: 'Come and see a man who told me everything I have done' (John 4:29). The invitation 'come and see' is a recurring motif in the Gospel of John.

The theme of 'abiding in' (μένω) Jesus is central to the Gospel of John, especially in John 15:4: 'Abide in me, and I will abide in you.' The disciples staying with Jesus that day is an early expression of this motif.

In John 14:23, Jesus says that he and the Father will come and make their home (μονή) with anyone who loves him — an elaboration on the theme of fellowship that begins with the disciples staying with Jesus.

In Revelation 3:20, Jesus stands at the door and knocks; whoever opens, he will go in to and share a meal with. This reflects the pattern from John 1:39, where Jesus invites into fellowship and they stay with him.

'Taste and see that the Lord is good' (Psalm 34:9). This Old Testament text expresses the invitation to personal experience of God's goodness, which forms the background for Jesus' call 'Come and see' in John 1:39.
